title: I always loved the scene where you shoot from the passenger seat of a getaway car, so I made a game where you never touch the wheel
author: office-canard
selftext:
There's a scene in the anime DEAD LEAVES I've always loved: someone else is driving the getaway car, and you're in the passenger seat shooting at everything chasing you. It looks wild, but what I loved about it was the trust underneath. You don't touch the wheel. You trust the driver completely, so you can give everything to the gun.



Then, while making an earlier game, I found that a pseudo-3D chase camera ran much more smoothly than I expected. I wondered if the two would fit together. They did.



In RIDING SHOTGUN, the car drives itself. You don't steer and you don't brake. You aim and fire.



\- Bikes, chase cars and gunmen close in from behind

\- The camera pulls back, so when you hit one car, you watch the ones behind it pile into it

\- The road swerves and your aim swings with it

\- 10 episodes, from city streets to snowbound mountain roads



Because the core never changes (a car that drives itself, an aim that sways, a road that won't slow down), I could pile any movie scene I wanted to shoot on top of it. A boss that's an old couple in a sidecar, charging head-on for a half-second shootout as you pass. Shooting a helicopter down from the roof of a moving car. Riders straight out of Fury Road.



The story came last. At some point the driver became a young man who loves her, and the back seat filled up with a bride in her wedding dress and a shotgun across her lap. It's a nod to the ending of The Graduate. But what made that ending famous was the doubt on their faces afterward, so I gave that doubt to the driver. Between stages, instead of a mission briefing, he lists the things he loved about her. Half love letter, half a man trying to convince himself he did the right thing. Right next to him, the bride doesn't share any of that doubt. She just shoots everything that moves.



How AI fit in: Claude wrote the code. Claude also wrote the "I loved..." lines the driver says between stages, all 499 of them. The art was made with Gemini.
